notes.title: Start here: Agora is a shop, read through five one-pagers
notes.body:
Agora is an online store backend (ASP.NET Core, EF Core) with a React front end, built sprint by sprint as a course. Each important idea has a one-page explainer in `docs/concepts/`. This quest uses five of them:

1. `lost-update.md`: two admins editing the same product.
2. `identity-vs-resource.md`: the login cookie versus the cart cookie.
3. `authn-vs-authz.md`: "who are you" versus "may you do this", and the status codes.
4. `value-objects.md`: why money is a type and not a `decimal`.
5. `the-clock.md`: why the current time must be passed in.

Each page ends with "Try it" or "Prove it" exercises and names the files that implement the idea. Read a page, then open those files; most questions here point at one method in them.

excerpts.quote: **One-pager · Sprint 03 · pairs with ADR 0005**

readMore.why: How the course expects you to study each sprint.
The decision record behind the lost-update page.

notes.title: Core idea: read, change, write back is a race
notes.body:
Many requests follow the same pattern: load a row, change something, save it. If two people do this at the same time on the same row, the second save can erase the first one without any error. This is called a lost update.

The usual fix is a version number on the row. The client sends back the version it read, and the server only accepts the save if the row has not moved on. Read `lost-update.md` and then follow the version check from the domain class through the use case to the database configuration. Notice that there are two separate checks, and ask why one would not be enough.

excerpts.quote: what happens if someone else writes between my read and my write?

readMore.why: The use case that compares versions.
Where Version becomes an EF concurrency token.

notes.title: Core idea: the same kind of token can mean very different things
notes.body:
Agora sets two cookies that look alike: random strings, hashed in the database. One proves who you are; the other only finds your shopping cart. The difference is not in the token but in what the server does when it receives it.

While reading `identity-vs-resource.md` and `authn-vs-authz.md`, keep three questions in mind: can a caller name something that is not theirs, what status code does a refusal use, and what happens when a request carries both cookies. Then read `CartLookup.cs`, which is only a few lines long.

excerpts.quote: **The privilege is not in the token. It is in the code path that reads it.**

readMore.why: The single place that decides which cart a request gets.
The 401 versus 403 rule in one table.

notes.title: A stale save is refused, not applied
notes.body:
The key is right. Ben read v3, but the product is at v4 after Alia's save. `UpdateProduct` checks `product.Version != expectedVersion` and throws a concurrency conflict, which the API turns into 409 with the current row, so his UI can show what changed.

- A silent overwrite is the last-write-wins bug the page describes.
- Agora does not merge edits; the user decides after seeing the 409.
- The status is 409 with a `current` member, not an empty 412.

excerpts.quote: if (product.Version != expectedVersion)
Ben's save is **rejected with `409 Conflict`**, not silently applied.

notes.title: Why the version is a plain int
notes.body:
The key is right. The tests run on SQLite, which has neither SQL Server's `rowversion` nor Postgres's `xmin`. If the database maintained the token, the concurrency behaviour would be untested on the very provider the suite uses. An explicit `int` that the domain increments works the same everywhere.

- The page does not mention leaking a clock; rowversion is a counter anyway.
- The reason is testing on SQLite, not an EF limitation with Postgres.
- Clients never choose the version; the domain increments it.

excerpts.quote: the test suite runs on **SQLite**, which has neither
Every edit bumps Version, so a stale editor

notes.title: Two gates for the same rule
notes.body:
The key is right. The in-code comparison catches the common case: a client that read an old version. But two requests can both pass that check before either commits. Marking `Version` as a concurrency token makes EF add the loaded value to the UPDATE's WHERE clause, so the late writer affects zero rows and gets `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`, translated into the same 409.

- The check runs in every build.
- The domain increments Version; EF does not generate it.
- The `current` row in the 409 comes from the exception handler, not from the token.

excerpts.quote: EF's concurrency token
builder.Property(p => p.Version).IsConcurrencyToken().IsRequired();

notes.title: The identity you proved beats the token you were handed
notes.body:
The key is right. `CartLookup` checks `currentUser.IsAuthenticated` first. If the user is signed in, it returns `FindActiveByUserAsync(currentUser.UserId, ...)` and never looks at the cart cookie. Only an anonymous request is resolved by the token hash.

- Preferring the token would let a stale or stolen cart cookie hand a customer someone else's cart.
- Merging happens once, at login (ADR 0007), not on every request.
- No 409 is involved; the lookup simply ignores the cookie.

excerpts.quote: return await carts.FindActiveByUserAsync(currentUser.UserId, cancellationToken);
**the identity wins**

notes.title: A method you decline to write is a door you cannot leave open
notes.body:
The key is right. `ICartRepository` offers `FindActiveByUserAsync` and `FindActiveByTokenHashAsync`, nothing that takes a cart id. No route accepts a cart id and no DTO carries one. A cart is always found by who you are, so nothing can ask for another person's cart.

- EF can look up any primary key; the omission is a design choice.
- No in-memory cache is involved.
- The page presents the missing method as the whole cost of the pattern, not as something admins get elsewhere.

excerpts.quote: Task<Cart?> FindActiveByUserAsync(Guid userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
`ICartRepository` has no `FindByIdAsync`, deliberately.

notes.title: One answer for every kind of "not yours"
notes.body:
The key is right. Line operations look the line up inside the caller's own cart; a stranger's line id is not in that list, so the use case throws `NotFoundException("cart line", lineId)`, a 404, the same as for a typo.

- A 403 would confirm that the line exists, an oracle for probing ids.
- 401 is for "logging in would fix it"; that is not the case here.
- Cart endpoints indeed skip `RequireUser`, but the line is still not found.

excerpts.quote: throw new NotFoundException("cart line", lineId);
A `403` says *this exists and you may not have it*.

notes.title: Authentication is checked before authorization
notes.body:
The key is right. `RequireRole` starts with `RequireUser()`, which throws `UnauthenticatedException` (401) for an anonymous caller. The role check only runs for a known user.

- 403 is for a signed-in user without the role: logging in would not help them.
- Agora uses 404 to hide resources you do not own, not admin routes.
- This is an API; it answers with a status code, not a redirect.

excerpts.quote: authentication FIRST (401), authorization SECOND (403).
"Would logging in fix it?" **Yes → 401. No → 403.**

notes.title: Money rounds half to even
notes.body:
The key is right. `Money.Of` is `new(Math.Round(amount, currency.MinorUnits, Rounding), currency)` and `Rounding` is `MidpointRounding.ToEven`. USD has two minor digits; 0.125 is exactly halfway between 0.12 and 0.13, and the even neighbour is 0.12.

- Away-from-zero would give 0.13; Agora chose banker's rounding.
- Money is rounded to the currency's minor units at the door, so three decimals never survive.
- Rounding is applied, not refused; no exception.

excerpts.quote: public const MidpointRounding Rounding = MidpointRounding.ToEven;
new(Math.Round(amount, currency.MinorUnits, Rounding), currency);

notes.title: One gate for every money operation
notes.body:
The key is right. Every binary operation on `Money` goes through `SameCurrencyAs`, which returns the other value only if the currencies are equal and otherwise throws `DomainRuleException("Cannot combine USD and EUR without an exchange rate.")`.

- Money has no exchange-rate source; it refuses instead of guessing.
- It never silently keeps one currency.
- There is no mixed-currency value; the type makes that state unrepresentable.

excerpts.quote: Cannot combine {Currency} and {other.Currency} without an exchange rate.
usd.Add(eur); // throws: "Cannot combine USD and EUR without an exchange rate."

notes.title: A ratio is not an amount of money
notes.body:
The key is right. `SavedPercent` divides savings by list price, both in the same currency. The currency cancels, leaving a pure number, so it returns a plain number (an `int` percentage in the current code) instead of `Money`. A `Money` percentage would be a category error.

- Money does allow negative amounts; a refund is negative money.
- Serialisation is not the reason; DTO mapping unwraps Money anyway.
- Precision is not the reason either; the result is rounded to a whole percent.

excerpts.quote: money by money CANCELS the currency
divides money by money and returns a plain `decimal` — deliberately.

notes.title: Put the rule where the rule is true
notes.body:
The key is right. `Product.ValidPrice` throws `DomainRuleException("Product price cannot be negative.")`. The rule belongs to products, because money in general can be negative: a refund is negative money.

- Putting it in `Money.Of` would block refunds, a legitimate use.
- The domain enforces it on every path, not only one HTTP validator.
- The EF configurations define no check constraint; the rule lives in the domain.

excerpts.quote: throw new DomainRuleException("Product price cannot be negative.");
`Money` permits a negative amount — a refund *is* negative money.

notes.title: Two functions, two clocks, two answers
notes.body:
The key is right. The page shows the price through `IsActiveAt(instant)`, which takes the moment as a parameter, while the badge used `IsActive()`, which fetched the time itself. They disagreed, and the ambient one was wrong; it was also the one with no tests, because you cannot tell it what "now" is.

- The browser only formats instants it was given.
- No cache is involved in the story.
- Both used the same price; the disagreement was about the time.

excerpts.quote: One took the instant as a parameter. The other fetched it itself.
`IsActive()` — the ambient one — had none at all
It shipped a flash sale whose badge appeared nine hours late while the price was already

notes.title: .DateTime throws the offset away
notes.body:
The key is right. `2026-08-04T09:00+09:00` is one instant. Its `.DateTime` property keeps the clock reading, 09:00, and drops the `+09:00`, so you get "nine o'clock somewhere unstated". Comparing that to the server's wall clock compares two local numbers about nothing.

- Converting to UTC would be `.UtcDateTime`; `.DateTime` does not convert.
- The server's timezone is not attached; the result has no zone.
- No exception is thrown for any offset.

excerpts.quote: Its `.DateTime` is **the number nine**
window.Starts.DateTime
